# Deploy Notify

One job: POST a short "deployed <version>" note to the team's chat
webhook at the end of a release.

## Usage

    ./notify.sh 1.4.2
    ./notify.sh 1.4.2 --webhook https://hooks.example.com/services/deploy

The webhook defaults to `https://hooks.example.com/services/deploy`
(override with `--webhook`). The version string is posted as
`{"version": ...}`; the response is ignored. No retry queue, no state
on disk.

--- notify.sh ---
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# POST a one-line deploy notification to the team chat webhook.
set -euo pipefail

WEBHOOK="https://hooks.example.com/services/deploy"

if [ $# -lt 1 ]; then
  echo "usage: notify.sh <version> [--webhook URL]" >&2
  exit 64
fi

VERSION="$(printf '%s' "$1" | sed 's/\\/\\\\/g; s/"/\\"/g')"
shift

while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --webhook) WEBHOOK="${2:?--webhook needs a URL}"; shift 2 ;;
    *) echo "unknown option: $1" >&2; exit 64 ;;
  esac
done

curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data "{\"version\": \"$VERSION\"}" "$WEBHOOK" >/dev/null

</skill-instructions>

raw_response:
TCP provides reliable, ordered, connection‑oriented delivery with error checking and retransmission, while UDP offers a lightweight, connectionless service that sends datagrams without guarantees of arrival or order. Consequently, TCP is suited for applications needing data integrity (e.g., web browsing, email), whereas UDP favors low latency and speed for real‑time uses like video streaming or online gaming.
